---
title: "Autocorrelation Prewhitening Under Fast-TR Event Designs"
subtitle: "Why two-pass REML AR(p) cascades outperform raw-residual lag tapering when task designs carry dozens of trial predictors"
---

## Overview: Why Not Use Nonparametric Lag Tapering?

A natural question from investigators familiar with classical univariate fMRI packages—especially FSL's FILM prewhitening ([Woolrich et al., 2001](https://doi.org/10.1006/nimg.2001.0931))—is why `estimate_crossrun_hrf()` fits a **two-pass parametric restricted-maximum-likelihood (REML) $\text{AR}(p)$ cascade** rather than tapering sample autocorrelations of ordinary least-squares (OLS) residuals with a Tukey cosine window.

At slow repetition times ($\text{TR} = 2.5\text{--}3.0\text{ s}$) under low-rank condition-averaged block or event GLMs, nonparametric residual lag tapering is simple and effective. In modern fast-TR ($\text{TR} \le 1.0\text{ s}$) single-trial analyses, however, two structural pressures arise simultaneously:

1. **Unmodeled neurovascular shape variation contaminates residual autocorrelation:** If noise is estimated in a single pass under an assumed canonical HRF, any region with a faster or slower hemodynamic peak leaves systematic task-locked waves in the residuals—driving estimated $\text{AR}(1)$ persistence $\widehat{\rho}$ artificially toward its stationarity ceiling (`0.90`).
2. **High-rank trial designs distort raw-residual autocorrelations:** Projecting dozens of free per-trial predictors out of a 300–400-volume run induces substantial negative finite-sample projection bias in raw OLS sample autocorrelations ($\operatorname{Cov}(r) = M_X \Sigma M_X^\top \neq \Sigma$), which cosine lag tapering shrinks toward zero rather than debiasing.

::: {.callout-note}
### Core Methodological Question & Connection to the Pipeline
*How can we separate regional HRF shape mismatch from genuine physiological autocorrelation—and keep both correlation shape $\Sigma_{\text{cor}}$ and marginal observation scale $\sigma_{\text{obs}}$ calibrated when propagating trial covariance $\Omega_{r,\tau}$?*

This chapter provides the statistical rationale and empirical benchmarks behind [**Step 1 (`estimate_crossrun_hrf()`)**](../medusa_step1_hrf_noise.qmd) and [**Step 2 (`deconvolve_crossrun_hrf(..., scaling = "noise_sd")`)**](../../medusa_step2_deconvolution/medusa_step2_deconvolution.qmd).
:::

---

## 1. Revisiting Woolrich et al. (2001) in the Fast-TR Single-Trial Regime

Woolrich, Ripley, Brady, and Smith (2001) established three enduring principles for fMRI temporal noise modeling: (a) mean-model misspecification spills directly into apparent serial correlation, (b) noisy voxelwise autocorrelation estimates benefit substantially from local spatial regularization within tissue classes, and (c) prewhitening requires coherent variance and correlation structure. In FILM, sample residual autocorrelations $\widehat{r}(\ell)$ are stabilized by multiplying lags $0 \le \ell < M$ by a smooth Tukey cosine window:

$$
\widehat{r}_T(\ell) =
\begin{cases}
\tfrac{1}{2}\bigl\{1 + \cos(\pi \ell / M)\bigr\}\widehat{r}(\ell), & 0 \le \ell < M, \\
0, & \ell \ge M.
\end{cases}
$$

When translating that estimator from condition-level GLMs at $\text{TR} = 3\text{ s}$ to trial-resolved deconvolution at $\text{TR} = 0.65\text{--}1.0\text{ s}$, two physical and algebraic properties change:

1. **Physical time span of a fixed lag window shrinks with TR:** A window of $M = 15$ lags spans $45\text{ s}$ at $\text{TR} = 3.0\text{ s}$, comfortably covering hemodynamic and Mayer-wave persistence, whereas the same 15 lags span less than $10\text{ s}$ at $\text{TR} = 0.65\text{ s}$. Widening $M$ in volume units accumulates estimation variance across dozens of lag parameters.
2. **Subspace projection bias scales with design rank:** Let $X_r$ collect the run's free trial predictors and low-frequency drift basis, and let $M_X = I - X_r(X_r^\top X_r)^{-1}X_r^\top$ denote the residual-forming projection matrix. Even under known true covariance $\Sigma$, raw OLS residuals $e_{\text{OLS}} = M_X y_r$ have covariance $M_X \Sigma M_X^\top$ rather than $\Sigma$. When $X_r$ occupies 25–40 degrees of freedom per run, raw sample autocorrelations dip systematically negative at intermediate lags (visible in green in @fig-woolrich-acf, even on a pure null parcel with zero neural signal). Multiplying $\widehat{r}(\ell)$ by a cosine taper dampens long lags without removing that negative subspace dip.

---

## 2. How MEDuSA Translates and Extends These Principles

Rather than tapering raw OLS residuals under a fixed canonical HRF, `medusa` separates neurovascular timing from serial correlation in two stages while accounting analytically for the residual subspace $M_X$:

| Noise-modeling principle | How `medusa` implements it | Why it matters downstream |
|:---|:---|:---|
| **Decouple HRF shape mismatch from residual persistence** | **Two-pass target-excluding REML refit** in `estimate_crossrun_hrf()`: Pass 1 estimates preliminary whitening under a canonical HRF plus temporal derivatives; once each parcel's HRF is learned *out of sample* from non-target runs $s \ne r$, Pass 2 refits run $r$'s $\text{AR}(p)$ noise model conditioned on the learned HRF while keeping HRF selection strictly frozen | Eliminates task-locked shape residuals in fast- or slow-HRF regions without circularity on the target run. |
| **Account for high-rank trial projection loss** | Profile REML $\text{AR}(1)$ likelihood evaluated directly on the projected subspace $M_X$, paired with projection-debiased residual $\text{AR}(q)$ Yule–Walker refinement (up to cascaded $\text{AR}(3)$) | Avoids the negative mid-lag autocorrelation dip induced by high-rank event designs while keeping the parameter count compact across TRs. |
| **Share noise information spatially without cancelling signed signals** | Pools REML log-likelihood profiles across voxels within anatomical parcels (`pooling = "parcel"`) or local autocorrelation-concordant cortical neighborhoods (`pooling = "graph"`) rather than averaging raw BOLD traces | Voxels with positive, negative, or null task responses contribute constructively to noise estimation while pial-rim pulsatility stays isolated from deep gray matter. |
| **Keep correlation shape and marginal amplitude coherent** | `deconvolve_crossrun_hrf(..., scaling = "noise_sd")` estimates outlier-trimmed, leverage-adjusted GLS innovation scale under the Pass-2 HRF and $\text{AR}(p)$ model, converting innovation SD analytically into stationary marginal `noise_sd` ($\sigma_{\text{obs}}$) | Prevents compensating errors between $\sigma_{\text{obs}}^2$ and $\Sigma_{\text{cor}}$ inside propagated trial covariance $\Omega_{r,\tau} = \sigma_{\text{obs}}^2 B_{r,\tau}\Sigma_{\text{cor}}B_{r,\tau}^\top$. |

---

## 3. Benchmark 1: Recovering True Autocorrelation Under Vascular Heterogeneity

To isolate these two mechanisms, consider the three-run fast-TR benchmark from [Step 1](../medusa_step1_hrf_noise.qmd) ($R = 3$ runs, $\text{TR} = 0.65\text{ s}$, $T_r = 360$ volumes, 24 jittered events per run, and 8 voxels each in a `Fast` HRF parcel, a `Slow` HRF parcel, and a pure `Null` parcel, generated under cascaded $\text{AR}(3)$ noise with $\rho = 0.65, \psi_1 = 0.20, \psi_2 = -0.30$). We compare four noise estimators on identical data:

1. **Single-pass canonical HRF:** Parametric REML $\text{AR}(p)$ noise fit locked to a fixed canonical HRF with no post-selection refit.
2. **Two-pass REML refit (`medusa`):** `estimate_crossrun_hrf()`, refitting run $r$'s $\text{AR}(p)$ cascade under the cross-run selected HRF.
3. **Oracle generating HRF:** Parametric REML $\text{AR}(p)$ conditioned on the exact generating HRF of each parcel.
4. **Raw-residual Tukey lag tapers ($M \in \{10, 15, 28\}$):** Pooled cosine-tapered sample residual autocorrelations under either the canonical or cross-run selected HRF.

@tbl-woolrich-acf reports the root-mean-square error (RMSE) of the implied autocorrelation function across lags 1–24 (`0.65–15.6 s`), averaged over runs:

```{r}
#| label: tbl-woolrich-acf
#| tbl-cap: "Implied noise autocorrelation RMSE across lags 1–24 (0.65–15.6 s; lower is better) comparing single-pass canonical HRF, two-pass REML refit, oracle HRF, and raw-residual Tukey lag tapers."
#| echo: false
a <- read.csv("diagnostic_summary.csv")
methods <- c(
  "Canonical_HRF", "Current_MEDuSA", "Oracle_true_HRF",
  "Tukey10_canonical", "Tukey15_canonical", "Tukey15_selected", "Tukey28_selected"
)
labels <- c(
  "Single-pass canonical HRF", "Two-pass REML refit (MEDuSA)", "Oracle generating HRF",
  "Tukey M=10 (canonical)", "Tukey M=15 (canonical)", "Tukey M=15 (selected HRF)", "Tukey M=28 (selected HRF)"
)
x <- sapply(methods, function(m) {
  z <- subset(a, method == m)
  setNames(z$acf_RMSE_1_24, z$parcel)[c("Fast", "Slow", "Null")]
})
rownames(x) <- c("Fast HRF parcel", "Slow HRF parcel", "Null parcel")
colnames(x) <- labels
knitr::kable(x, digits = 3)
```

![Implied Run 1 noise autocorrelation functions across the `Fast`, `Null`, and `Slow` parcels. MEDuSA's two-pass REML refit (blue dotted) tracks the generating covariance (black solid) across all three vascular regimes, whereas locking noise estimation to a single-pass canonical HRF (amber dashed) inflates apparent persistence whenever the true HRF is faster or slower, and raw-residual Tukey tapering (green dot-dash) dips negative from trial-design projection bias even in the `Null` parcel.](noise_comparison.png){#fig-woolrich-acf width="100%" fig-alt="Three-panel ACF plot across Fast, Null, and Slow parcels comparing generating covariance, single-pass canonical HRF, MEDuSA two-pass REML refit, and raw-residual Tukey M=15 taper."}

Two conclusions emerge directly from @tbl-woolrich-acf and @fig-woolrich-acf:

- **Refitting noise under the cross-fitted HRF removes vascular spillover:** Under a single-pass canonical HRF, unmodeled early or late BOLD lobes inflate apparent autocorrelation (`RMSE = 0.260` in `Fast`, `0.314` in `Slow`). Refitting $\text{AR}(p)$ parameters under the out-of-sample selected HRF reduces ACF RMSE more than thirtyfold to **`0.006`** and **`0.008`**—matching the oracle-HRF benchmark (`0.006` and `0.008`) with zero target-run circularity.
- **Subspace REML avoids high-rank projection bias:** Even when supplied the learned HRF (`Tukey M=15 (selected HRF)`), raw-residual lag tapering retains an order-of-magnitude higher error (`0.090–0.100`)—including **`0.100` vs. `0.011`** on the pure `Null` parcel—because projecting out 24 trial regressors plus drift biases raw sample autocorrelations downward across lags 2–8 (`1.3–5.2 s`).

---

## 4. Benchmark 2: Why Diagonal SEs Can Look Right While Full Covariance Is Wrong

For downstream inference in Steps 3–6, temporal autocorrelation matters through the **propagated trial readout covariance** $\Omega_{r,\tau} = \sigma_{\text{obs}}^2 B_{r,\tau}\Sigma_{\text{cor}}B_{r,\tau}^\top$. Evaluating a fixed deconvolution and onset-readout operator across the simulated schedule, @tbl-woolrich-var compares the single-pass canonical noise fit against the two-pass REML refit under both a standalone second-difference scale estimator (`d2`) and MEDuSA's covariance-consistent Winsorized GLS marginal scale (`GLS`, `scaling = "noise_sd"`):

```{r}
#| label: tbl-woolrich-var
#| tbl-cap: "Calibration of marginal noise SD, diagonal trial readout SEs, and full trial-by-trial covariance matrices (ideal ratios = 1.000; ideal relative Frobenius error = 0.000)."
#| echo: false
v <- read.csv("variance_check.csv")
z <- aggregate(. ~ parcel + method, v[, setdiff(names(v), "run")], mean)
z <- z[order(match(z$parcel, c("Fast", "Slow", "Null")), match(z$method, c("Canonical_HRF", "Current_MEDuSA"))), ]
knitr::kable(
  data.frame(
    Parcel = z$parcel,
    `Noise correlation model` = ifelse(z$method == "Canonical_HRF", "Single-pass canonical HRF", "Two-pass REML refit (MEDuSA)"),
    `GLS SD / true` = z$median_gls_SD_ratio,
    `2nd-diff SD / true` = z$median_d2_SD_ratio,
    `Trial SE / true (known SD)` = z$median_known_scale_SE_ratio,
    `Trial SE / true (GLS SD)` = z$median_gls_SE_ratio,
    `Full Cov Frobenius Err` = z$median_full_cov_error_gls,
    check.names = FALSE
  ),
  digits = 3,
  row.names = FALSE
)
```

@tbl-woolrich-var illustrates a subtle diagnostic trap: under the single-pass canonical HRF model, two large errors partially cancel along the diagonal. Its overly persistent correlation matrix $\Sigma_{\text{cor}}$ under-predicts trial SEs by nearly half when true marginal SD is known (`0.484–0.564`), while unmodeled HRF shape residuals inflate estimated marginal `GLS SD` more than twofold (`2.038–2.281`). Their product leaves diagonal SE ratios looking deceptively benign (`1.10–1.14`), even though the **full $m \times m$ trial covariance matrix** suffers `21–28%` relative Frobenius distortion—corrupting off-diagonal cross-trial and cross-lag correlation estimates needed by Step 4 ZCA whitening and Step 5 `medusa_multilag_infer()`. Pairing the two-pass REML refit with `scaling = "noise_sd"` calibrates *both* pieces (`GLS SD / true = 1.01–1.05`, known-scale `SE / true = 0.98–1.01`), cutting full covariance matrix error to **`4.3–7.5%`**.

---

## 5. Implications for Applied MEDuSA Analyses

| Modeling choice | Recommended setting | Takeaway from this chapter |
|:---|:---|:---|
| **Spatial pooling of noise (`pooling`)** | `"parcel"` for homogeneous ROIs; `"graph"` on volumetric cortical ribbons | When anatomical parcels straddle CSF/pial borders and deep gray matter, `pooling = "graph"` ([Spatial Graph Pooling](../../medusa_spatial_parcel_pooling/medusa_spatial_parcel_pooling.qmd#sec-bilateral-noise)) weights local smoothing by autocorrelation concordance so vascular-rim pulsatility does not contaminate interior cortex ([Olszowy et al., 2019](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6428826/); [Parlak et al., 2023](https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/neuroscience/articles/10.3389/fnins.2022.1051424/full)). |
| **Autoregressive order (`ar_order`)** | `"auto"` (cascaded up to $\text{AR}(3)$) | Captures multiband serial correlation cleanly across $\text{TR} \in [0.65, 2.0]\text{ s}$; for ultra-fast acquisitions ($\text{TR} < 0.5\text{ s}$), include physiological nuisance regressors (`RETROICOR` / `aCompCor`) alongside `motion_bandstop_bpm`. |
| **Step 2 amplitude scaling (`scaling`)** | `"noise_sd"` (paired with `restore_scale = TRUE` in Step 3) | Anchors continuous deconvolution penalties and Step 3/4 propagated covariances to the Pass-2 GLS marginal observation noise SD rather than task-inflated total run variance. |
| **Cross-parcel noise vs. temporal whitening** | Retain `subject_epochs` for Step 6 (`shared_error = "auto"`) | Prewhitening within each parcel calibrates within-region $\Omega_{gg}$, whereas cross-parcel shared noise $\Omega_{ST}$ is captured separately via Step 2's task-free `noise_innovations` (see [Propagating BOLD Noise into Trial SEs](../../medusa_standard_errors_mmom.qmd)). |

<summary>Implementation Pointers & Reproduction</summary>

Inside `medusa`, the two-pass REML noise refit and covariance-consistent marginal noise scale are implemented in `R/crossrun_hrf.R` (`estimate_crossrun_hrf()`, `fit_crossrun_decon()`, `hrf_estimate_noise()`, `hrf_estimate_gls_noise_sd()`), with standalone second-difference fallback scaling in `R/deconvolve_reglin.R` (`estimate_decon_noise_sd()`).

To regenerate the benchmark tables and @fig-woolrich-acf from `book/medusa_step1_hrf_noise/woolrich_review/` (after running `../simulate_step1.R`):

```bash
Rscript compare_noise.R
Rscript variance_check.R
Rscript plot_comparison.R
```
